questions.q: A team must point the zone apex `example.com` at an Application Load Balancer. Which record should they create?

options.t: A CNAME record to the ALB DNS name
options.why: Wrong: a CNAME cannot be created at the zone apex.

options.t: An alias A record to the ALB
options.why: Right: alias records work at the apex, point to AWS resources, and alias queries to AWS resources are free.

options.t: An NS record to the ALB
options.why: Wrong: NS records delegate zones, they do not map a name to a load balancer.

options.t: A TXT record holding the ALB name
options.why: Wrong: TXT records are not followed by resolvers to reach a target.

questions.explain: Apex plus AWS resource means an alias record.
questions.remember: Zone apex or a free-query pointer to an AWS resource (ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, S3 website) → alias A/AAAA, never CNAME.
variants: Name is a subdomain pointing to a Redshift or RDS endpoint → CNAME (alias does not target them).
Target is another record in the same hosted zone → alias also works.
Cost matters for queries → alias queries to AWS resources are free, CNAME queries are billed.

questions.q: An application must switch automatically to a static S3 maintenance site when its primary Region stops responding. Which Route 53 setup meets this?

options.t: Weighted records with weights 100 and 0
options.why: Wrong: weights do not react to failure; a health check must also be involved and weight 0 sends no traffic.

options.t: Failover records with a health check on the primary
options.why: Right: Route 53 returns the secondary only when the primary health check fails; the secondary may be an S3 static page.

options.t: Latency-based records to one Region
options.why: Wrong: latency routing picks the lowest latency Region, not a passive standby.

options.t: Simple record with two values
options.why: Wrong: simple routing has no per-value health and returns values in random order.

questions.explain: Active-passive DR uses failover routing with a health check on the primary.
questions.remember: Active-passive with automatic cutover → failover routing; a health check on the primary is required.
variants: Both Regions serve users at once → latency-based routing with health checks.
Gradual migration old to new → weighted routing with low TTL.
Operators must control failover safely → Application Recovery Controller routing controls.

questions.q: Users worldwide should reach the AWS Region with the best network performance, and an unhealthy Region must be skipped. Which policy fits?

options.t: Geolocation routing
options.why: Wrong: it routes by the user's country or continent, not by measured latency.

options.t: Latency-based routing with health checks
options.why: Right: it picks the Region with the lowest latency to the user's network and skips unhealthy records.

options.t: Multivalue answer routing
options.why: Wrong: it returns up to 8 healthy records without choosing the fastest.

options.t: Weighted routing
options.why: Wrong: weights are fixed percentages and ignore latency.

questions.explain: Lowest latency Region means latency-based routing.
questions.remember: Fastest Region for the user → latency-based; where the user is (rules, compliance) → geolocation.
variants: EU users must only get EU endpoints → geolocation with a default record.
Shift load between Regions by distance with a bias → geoproximity.
Route known corporate CIDRs to a specific endpoint → IP-based routing with a CIDR collection.

questions.q: A health check must monitor an ALB that sits in private subnets and is not reachable from the internet. How should failover be driven?

options.t: An HTTPS endpoint health check against the private IP
options.why: Wrong: Route 53 health checkers are on the public internet and cannot reach private IPs.

options.t: A calculated health check with no children
options.why: Wrong: a calculated check only combines other checks.

options.t: A CloudWatch alarm health check on a metric of the resource
options.why: Right: its status follows the alarm, so private resources can be monitored through metrics.

options.t: A TCP health check from a VPC security group
options.why: Wrong: security groups do not run Route 53 health checks.

questions.explain: Private resources need CloudWatch alarm based health checks (or a public health endpoint).
questions.remember: Private endpoint needing a Route 53 health check → CloudWatch alarm health check or a public health endpoint.
variants: Public ALB or CloudFront alias → use Evaluate Target Health instead of a separate check.
Combine several checks with AND/OR → calculated health check (up to 255 children).
Endpoint check must allow the health checker IP ranges in firewalls.

questions.q: On-premises ETL servers must resolve the private DNS name of an interface VPC endpoint and a private hosted zone over a VPN. Which design is required?

options.t: A Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule
options.why: Wrong: outbound sends VPC queries out to on-prem DNS, the opposite direction.

options.t: A Resolver inbound endpoint plus a conditional forwarder on the corporate DNS
options.why: Right: on-prem DNS forwards queries into the VPC resolver, which can see private zones and endpoint names.

options.t: A public hosted zone with the private IPs
options.why: Wrong: exposes private data to the internet and still is not the supported hybrid pattern.

options.t: DNS Firewall rule group
options.why: Wrong: it filters outbound VPC queries and does not resolve names for on-prem.

questions.explain: On-prem to AWS names needs an inbound endpoint.
questions.remember: On-prem resolving AWS private names → Resolver inbound endpoint; AWS resolving on-prem names → outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule.
variants: VPC workloads must resolve corp.example.com → outbound endpoint plus forwarding rule shared with RAM.
Endpoints need at least 2 IPs in 2 AZs and security groups allowing TCP/UDP 53.
Do not forward the same domain in both directions (loops).

questions.q: A company has 800 VPCs across many accounts that must all resolve the same private hosted zones and Resolver rules. A single private hosted zone can be associated with only 300 VPCs. What is the best fix?

options.t: Create 3 copies of each zone and associate manually
options.why: Wrong: duplicates records and adds operational burden.

options.t: Route 53 Profiles shared with AWS RAM
options.why: Right: Profiles bundle PHZ associations and Resolver rules and apply them to many VPCs and accounts.

options.t: Request a Resolver inbound endpoint per VPC
options.why: Wrong: endpoints are limited to 4 per Region and do not solve association limits.

options.t: A public hosted zone
options.why: Wrong: loses private resolution.

questions.explain: Profiles solve the 300-VPC association limit and centralize DNS governance.
questions.remember: Many VPCs/accounts needing the same PHZs and rules → Route 53 Profiles shared via RAM.
variants: Cross-account association of a few VPCs → authorization then association.
Share forwarding rules only → RAM share the Resolver rule.
Profiles also bundle DNS Firewall rule groups and query logging configs.

questions.q: A security team must block VPC workloads from resolving known malware and botnet command-and-control domains and keep a record of blocked lookups. Which services combine to do this?

options.t: Security groups with deny rules
options.why: Wrong: security groups only allow and do not filter DNS names.

options.t: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall with managed domain lists, plus Resolver query logging
options.why: Right: DNS Firewall blocks outbound DNS queries by domain list and query logs record the activity.

options.t: DNSSEC signing
options.why: Wrong: it validates authenticity of responses and does not block domains.

options.t: A private hosted zone only
options.why: Wrong: does not filter malicious domains.

questions.explain: DNS Firewall filters outbound DNS; query logs give the audit trail.
questions.remember: Block or alert on domains queried from a VPC → Resolver DNS Firewall; audit trail → Resolver query logging.
variants: Authenticity of public zone answers → DNSSEC.
Rule might block valid domains → start with ALERT before BLOCK.
Manage firewall policy across accounts → Firewall Manager.

questions.q: A data platform team sees instances inside a VPC resolve `data.example.com` to a different address than the internet does, with the same zone name existing publicly and privately. What explains this and what is it called?

options.t: Latency routing; multi-Region
options.why: Wrong: latency policy is not tied to VPC association.

options.t: A private hosted zone with the same name associated with the VPC; split-horizon DNS
options.why: Right: inside associated VPCs the private zone answers (even NXDOMAIN for missing names).

options.t: DNSSEC validation; chain of trust
options.why: Wrong: DNSSEC does not change answers by location.

options.t: Geoproximity bias; traffic flow
options.why: Wrong: that shifts traffic by geography, not by VPC.

questions.explain: Same-name public and private zones give split-horizon DNS.
questions.remember: Different answers inside the VPC than outside → private hosted zone with the same name (split-horizon).
variants: PHZ requires enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames on the VPC.
Name missing from the PHZ resolves NXDOMAIN inside the VPC.
Reach a SaaS endpoint privately by name → PHZ record to your interface endpoint.

questions.q: Spark executors on EMR make thousands of DNS lookups per second from one node and some lookups fail intermittently. What is the likely cause and fix?

options.t: The 1,024 packets per second per network interface limit to the VPC resolver; cache DNS and reduce lookups
options.why: Right: the limit is fixed and not adjustable, so reduce and cache lookups or spread across interfaces.

options.t: Hosted zone quota of 500; request an increase
options.why: Wrong: unrelated to per-lookup throttling.

options.t: Health check quota of 200
options.why: Wrong: health checks do not affect resolver lookups.

options.t: DNSSEC key rotation
options.why: Wrong: would cause validation failures, not intermittent throttling.

questions.explain: The VPC resolver is limited to 1,024 pps per ENI and cannot be raised.
questions.remember: Intermittent DNS failures under heavy load from one instance → 1,024 pps per ENI resolver limit; cache and reduce lookups.
variants: Resolver endpoint IP nearing capacity → add ENIs when above 50% of about 10,000 QPS.
API change throttling → batch ChangeResourceRecordSets and back off.
Stale answers after change → lower TTL before cutover.

questions.q: A company is migrating traffic from an old stack to a new one and wants to shift 10% first, then increase it, while limiting how long clients cache old answers. Which choices apply? Choose 2.

options.t: Weighted records with set identifiers
options.why: Right: weights control the percentage of traffic to each stack.

options.t: A low TTL before and during the cutover
options.why: Right: resolvers cache until TTL expires, so a low TTL lets weight changes take effect quickly.

options.t: Failover records with no health check
options.why: Wrong: failover needs a health check on the primary and switches only on failure.

options.t: Simple routing with two values
options.why: Wrong: returns values in random order with no control of percentages.

options.t: A CNAME at the zone apex
options.why: Wrong: not allowed at the apex.

questions.explain: Weighted routing plus a low TTL gives a gradual, fast-reacting cutover.
questions.remember: Gradual blue/green or canary shift → weighted routing with low TTL; lower TTL ahead of time, raise afterwards.
variants: Automatic switch only on failure → failover routing.
Weight 0 means no traffic unless every record has weight 0.
Routing-policy records need a set identifier.
